messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 28
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: European
- Relationship Status: Married
- Occupation: Financial Analyst
- Trauma Type: Child's life-threatening illness
- Pcl5: 75

At 28, he still speaks about the beginning of it as if the world changed direction in a single afternoon. He is a European man, married, and by training a financial analyst, someone accustomed to tracking risk, weighing probabilities, and keeping his emotions contained behind careful language and organized spreadsheets. Before his son became critically ill, he thinks of himself as steady, practical, and good in a crisis. He and his wife are newly settled into parenthood when their child develops a sudden, life-threatening illness that quickly moves them from ordinary routines into hospital rooms, alarms, and medical terms they barely understand.

He describes the first days as unreal. He remembers the brightness of the pediatric unit, the smell of antiseptic, the constant interruptions of nurses checking lines and monitors. He sits beside the small bed trying to make sense of numbers on screens, though he does not understand half of them. What he does understand is the fear in his wife’s face and the way the doctors’ voices change when they have something serious to say. He stays composed at first, asking questions, taking notes, and calculating odds in the same way he approaches work. But the logic he depends on fails him there. No amount of preparation seems to matter, and the helplessness lands hard. He cannot bargain with the illness, cannot work harder to fix it, cannot forecast his son’s recovery the way he forecasts market trends.

As the emergency stretches into days and then weeks, he becomes increasingly alert and exhausted. He sleeps in fragments, always listening for the next alarm or the sound of someone entering the room. Even after they go home, the hospital remains vivid in his mind. He says that certain sounds—the beeping of a monitor in a store, the hiss of a hospital oxygen tank on television, even a phone notification at night—can pull him back so quickly that he feels the same surge of panic in his chest. He startles easily, and his body seems to stay on guard long after the danger has passed. He checks his son repeatedly, watching for signs of breathing, color, movement, anything that might mean the illness is returning. At times he wakes in the middle of the night and stands over the crib or bed, frozen between relief and dread.

At work, he keeps functioning, but only at a cost. He remains punctual and technically competent, yet colleagues notice that he seems distant and preoccupied. He has difficulty concentrating in meetings and reads the same lines of a report several times without taking them in. He begins making small errors that would once have irritated him. He compensates by working longer hours and double-checking everything, but the effort leaves him tense and drained. He says he no longer trusts things to stay stable just because they have been stable before. That mistrust extends beyond his son’s health into everything: deadlines, plans, ordinary family routines, even happy moments that now feel fragile and provisional.

His relationship with his wife changes too. They share the same trauma, but they carry it differently. She wants to talk through what happened; he often turns inward and becomes quiet. He worries that if he lets himself feel too much, he will fall apart and no one will be left to manage what comes next. So he stays busy, watches, anticipates, and controls whatever he can. Beneath that control, however, there is grief and guilt. He wonders whether he missed early signs, whether he should have pushed for care sooner, whether there was some action he failed to take. Even when the child improves, he cannot fully believe in safety. He feels guilty for wanting his old life back because the memory of those nights in the hospital is still so close.

Now, months later, he describes living in a narrower emotional range. He is grateful his child is alive, but he does not experience relief in a simple way. Instead, he moves through the day with a constant internal strain, as though he is braced for another emergency. He avoids thinking too far ahead. He keeps checking, keeps planning, keeps himself occupied. When he does slow down, the images return: the tiny body under blankets, the harsh light, the fear that sat in the room with them. He presents as a man who has learned that catastrophe can arrive without warning and that love, for him, now includes the possibility of losing everything in an instant.
